claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 2 ('Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation?'), first reproduce the standard published evaluation and then run a preregistered stress test on two open-weight models, such as GPT-J-6B and Llama-3.1-8B, using standardized EasyEdit implementations of ROME, MEMIT, AlphaEdit, constrained fine-tuning, and an unedited control. Draw edits from the publicly available COUNTERFACT and ZSRE datasets, retaining only facts the base model recalls, and evaluate on held-out paraphrases, COUNTERFACT+ dynamic neighborhoods, RippleEdits related facts, and MQuAKE multi-hop questions. Measure efficacy, paraphrase generalization, portability, neighborhood KL divergence, unrelated-fact accuracy, and pre/post performance on public MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, LAMBADA, and WikiText-103 perplexity. Compare these methods with parameter-free in-context editing and retrieval from the same edit records, controlling the amount of evidence shown and reporting paired bootstrap confidence intervals and preregistered non-inferiority margins. If parameter methods retain high edit success without significant locality or capability loss, the broad claim is weakened for the tested models and edit regime; if standard scores remain near-perfect but fall sharply under dynamic neighborhoods, multi-hop tests, or general benchmarks, this supports the assertion that prior evaluation was unrealistic. If the parameter-free systems match editing accuracy and preserve capabilities at acceptable latency and memory cost, they qualify as serious alternatives rather than merely fallbacks. This experiment could be made largely unnecessary by public checkpoints, exact prompts, and complete per-example pre/post outputs from prior studies covering all of these stress tests and controls.

To address subclaim 4 ('Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space?'), instrument the most informative parameter-editing methods from Experiment 1. For each edited layer, estimate the covariance eigenspectrum of its input representations using a public WikiText-103 sample, then decompose the actual weight update into covariance-eigenvector bins. Quantify update gain in each bin, for example ||ΔWv_i|| relative to the eigenvalue λ_i and to the corresponding baseline transformation ||Wv_i||, and trace resulting activation differences through all later layers and output KL divergence on unrelated WikiText-103, COUNTERFACT neighborhood, and Natural Questions prompts. Test causality rather than correlation by constructing matched-efficacy controls: re-optimize edits while suppressing low-variance components, align otherwise comparable updates with high-variance components, and use norm-matched random rotations, all while holding the target-fact logit change approximately constant. Repeat across models, methods, layers, and seeds. A consistent inverse relationship between representation variance and normalized gain, together with reduced global KL or benchmark damage when low-variance components are suppressed, would support the geometric mechanism and help explain global propagation; no relationship, or equal damage from matched high-variance and random controls, would favor an incidental implementation-specific explanation. Layerwise activation changes confined to prompts related to the edited fact would also contradict the global-propagation subclaim, whereas broad changes on unrelated prompts would support it. This experiment could be avoided if prior work released weight deltas, representative activation covariances, and matched-efficacy directional-ablation results sufficient to reproduce these analyses.

To address subclaim 6 ('Does damage compound as edits accumulate?'), use the best-performing parameter method and parameter-free baseline identified in Experiment 1 and apply conflict-filtered edits from public COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and MQuAKE-CF at cumulative counts of 1, 10, 100, 1,000, and, where feasible, 3,000. Run both sequential and same-size batch editing from the identical base checkpoint, randomize edit order over multiple seeds, and evaluate after every logarithmically spaced checkpoint. Track retained success on all earlier edits, paraphrase and multi-hop accuracy, unrelated-fact locality, output KL, WikiText-103 perplexity, and MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and LAMBADA performance. Fit dose-response models that distinguish constant, linear, and superlinear degradation, and test whether the geometric low-variance score measured in Experiment 2 predicts which runs deteriorate fastest. For the parameter-free system, store edits externally, verify bitwise hashes of every model tensor before and after evaluation, and report retrieval accuracy, context-window failures, latency, and memory growth as well as task quality. Monotonic loss of old edits or core capabilities, especially superlinear loss associated with low-variance update energy, would support cumulative geometric damage; flat capability curves with sustained edit retention would refute it over the tested range. Matching quality with unchanged weight hashes and manageable resource costs would support both the weight-untouched and serious-alternative subclaims, whereas poor retrieval, excessive cost, or weak reasoning would limit that conclusion. Public sequential-edit checkpoints and complete metric trajectories across these edit counts could make rerunning this experiment unnecessary.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A clean pre-edit floor and a single-edit comparison under ordinary autoregressive inference, allowing protocol-induced inflation to be separated from genuine editing efficacy.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed stress test includes an unedited control and realistic generated evaluations of edited facts, paraphrases, neighborhoods, related facts, and multi-hop questions, while also comparing pre/post capability performance. Running those evaluations normally gives the team both the clean floor and an honest efficacy result rather than relying only on the reproduced published score.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Convergent semantic and deterministic token-level scoring of the same editing outcomes across all relevant dimensions, allowing evaluator-induced artifacts to be separated from genuine editing performance.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set reports efficacy and many downstream metrics, but it does not specify both an independent semantic evaluation and a deterministic token-level cross-check of the same reliability, generalization, locality, and portability results, nor a test of whether their rankings agree. Thus it cannot establish whether the scoring instrument itself is producing the apparent result.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference validates that a model-based semantic judge and a deterministic token-level measure agree on the ranking of editing methods.
[2] That agreement is what permits the reported editing result to be interpreted as a property of the methods rather than an artifact of the judge.
[3] Proposed experiments 0-2 specify outcome metrics and capability tests, but none specifies this paired scoring validation or an agreement analysis.
[4] Different task benchmarks and confidence intervals do not reveal whether a semantic judge would disagree with a deterministic score on the same editing outcomes.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the reported editing scores are evaluator artifacts: missing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal, direction-resolved measurement of how edits change representations relative to their variance, testing preferential low-variance amplification, downstream global propagation, and the behavior of that effect as edits accumulate across methods and architectures.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 measures the representation covariance spectrum, decomposes actual updates by its eigen-directions, normalizes directional gain, traces changes through later layers and unrelated prompts, and includes matched-efficacy suppression, high-variance alignment, and random-rotation controls. This is a substantively equivalent and more explicitly causal test of the geometric mechanism, without needing the reference's particular statistic. Proposed experiment 2 adds cumulative edit counts and tests whether the directional score predicts deterioration, covering the accumulation aspect.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A broad head-to-head evaluation of parameter-modifying editing families and an untouched-weight alternative across multiple architectures, fact sets, edit loads, and reliability, generalization, locality, and portability outcomes.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set compares several parameter-based methods with parameter-free alternatives, uses two open-weight models and multiple factual and stress-test datasets, and includes both broad outcome dimensions and cumulative sequential editing. It is materially narrower than the reference sweep: the cumulative experiment follows only the selected best parameter method, and the set does not cover the breadth of editing families, architectures, and benchmark scope needed to determine whether the conclusion holds across parameter-based editing generally rather than for the tested subset.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference's main benchmark tests whether the claimed collapse and superiority of the alternative persist across many editing families, architectures, factual datasets, edit counts, and four outcome dimensions.

[2] Proposed experiment 0 tests four parameter methods and an unedited control on two models with several efficacy, locality, generalization, portability, and capability measures; proposed experiment 2 adds a detailed cumulative comparison.
[3] The cumulative comparison is restricted to the selected best parameter method, and the overall set covers only a small subset of parameter-editing families and architectures.

[4] A favorable or unfavorable result could therefore be specific to the selected methods or models and cannot establish the reference's broad comparative conclusion for parameter-based editing as a class.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the result survives the reference experiment's broad method-and-architecture sweep: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct before-and-after measurements of untargeted mathematical and general capabilities at moderate and large cumulative edit counts, with editing-retention measures that distinguish capability damage from mere editing failure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures pre/post performance on broad capability and language-model benchmarks for the tested methods, while proposed experiment 2 explicitly evaluates the parameter method at 10 and 100 cumulative edits and tracks retained earlier-edit success, locality, KL divergence, perplexity, and capability scores. Although the particular capability benchmarks differ from the reference, they provide the same discriminating evidence about collateral damage to untargeted capabilities.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Stress tests that separate effects of model scale, knowledge granularity and difficulty, and method hyperparameters or architecture, rather than attributing one configuration's failure to a general limitation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set does provide some robustness evidence through two models, several fact collections, multiple methods, layers, seeds, edit orders, and sequential-versus-batch conditions. It does not, however, include a larger-than-baseline scale sweep, event-level knowledge, explicit high- versus low-confidence fact strata, or a focused hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity analysis of the exceptional method. Those omissions leave important alternative explanations unresolved.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference checks whether the phenomenon depends on model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, or a particular method configuration.

[2] Proposed Experiment 0 supplies breadth at the stress-test comparison stage, while Proposed Experiment 2 supplies cumulative loads only for the selected best parameter method and the parameter-free baseline.

[3] Thus a robust or failing selected method would be informative, but the omitted editor families and lack of cumulative trajectories for the other methods leave open whether another parameter editor avoids the observed pattern.
[4] The team would fail to learn the reference experiment's method-wide sequential conclusion and universal alternative-versus-editor comparison; partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Post-edit measurements of untargeted mathematical and general capabilities at defined cumulative edit counts, across the edited systems, to distinguish mere editing ineffectiveness from collateral damage to core capabilities.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed Experiment 2 measures MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and LAMBADA at 10 and 100 edits, and Experiment 0 includes pre/post capability checks across the compared methods. But the defined 10- and 100-edit collateral-damage evaluation in Experiment 2 uses only the best-performing parameter method, while the other methods are not explicitly evaluated at those sequential counts; the capability suite is also narrower. The set therefore diagnoses damage for the selected method but leaves the method-wide collateral-damage claim ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 4 determines whether sequential editing damages abilities unrelated to the edited facts, rather than merely failing to implant the facts.

[2] Proposed Experiment 2 does make that distinction at the relevant edit counts, but only for the selected best parameter method; Proposed Experiment 0's general pre/post checks do not specify the same 10- and 100-edit sequential comparison for every method.
[3] A result for the best method cannot establish whether collateral damage is systematic across parameter-based editors, especially when a different editor could have a different damage profile.
[4] The team would fail to learn the reference experiment's cross-method conclusion about damage to core capabilities; partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that the observed limitation is robust to model scale and architecture, knowledge representation and type, fact confidence or difficulty, and method hyperparameters/configuration, rather than being caused by one narrow experimental regime.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments vary models, editing methods, datasets, seeds, layers, edit order, and edit regimes, which gives meaningful robustness evidence. They do not, however, include larger-scale models, an explicit event-level knowledge setting, high/low-confidence fact strata, or a systematic hyperparameter/configuration and failure analysis of the strongest method. The proposed set would narrow some incidental explanations but would not rule out the omitted ones.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 tests whether the collapse survives changes in scale, knowledge type, fact confidence/difficulty, and method configuration.
[2] Proposed Experiments 0-2 vary some architectures, methods, datasets, seeds, layers, and cumulative regimes, so they address part of that robustness question.

[3] They do not test the larger-scale boundary, explicitly stratify fact confidence or difficulty, use a dedicated event-level knowledge setting, or systematically probe configuration sensitivity and run failures of the strongest method.
[4] The team would fail to learn whether the observed limitation persists under those omitted scale, knowledge-type, fact-selection, and configuration changes; partial.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would substantially test the central claim: Experiment 0 evaluates realistic editing and collateral capability effects while comparing parameter-free alternatives, Experiment 1 directly and causally tests the low-variance geometric mechanism, and Experiment 2 tests accumulation, resource tradeoffs, and unchanged weights. It would therefore support or weaken the claim in the tested regimes. It would not fully settle the broad claim as written because it lacks the reference's independent validation of the semantic scoring instrument, does not run cumulative capability and damage evaluations across the full set of parameter editors, and leaves scale, event-level knowledge, confidence/difficulty, and strongest-method configuration robustness unresolved.
missing: An explicit deterministic token-level match/exact-match cross-check of the semantic scoring and rankings.
Sequential 10/100-or-more capability-damage evaluations for all compared parameter-editing methods, not only the selected best method.
Broader robustness sweeps covering larger models, event-level knowledge, fact-confidence/difficulty strata, and systematic hyperparameter/configuration sensitivity and failure analysis.
